prompt.context_jp: そこで語られようとしているのは、この職場の技師長___抱える、生々しい家庭事情だった。
prompt.prompt_jp: そこで語られようとしているのは、この職場の技師長___抱える、生々しい家庭事情だった。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle that fits in the relative clause.

feedback.correct_en: Inside a relative clause ('family situation that the chief technician is dealing with'), the subject of the embedded verb 抱える takes が. は can't appear as the subject marker inside a noun-modifying clause here.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would try to set the chief technician as a sentence-level topic, breaking the relative clause. を would mark him as object, which doesn't fit 抱える's meaning here.

contrast_examples.en: the book he wrote (subject in relative clause → が)
He wrote a book (main-clause topic → は)

prompt.context_jp: 甘春総合病院の朝、放射線科技師室___はどこか落ち着かない空気が漂っていた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 放射線科技師室___はどこか落ち着かない空気が漂っていた。
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the particle that marks where the atmosphere exists.

feedback.correct_en: 漂う (to drift/linger) describes existence/state in a location, so に marks the place where the atmosphere lingers. で would imply an action is taking place there.
feedback.incorrect_en: で marks where active events occur; 漂う here describes a static state. を doesn't mark location.

contrast_examples.en: Silence lingers in the room (state → に)
Hold a meeting in the room (action → で)

prompt.context_jp: 湯呑から___鼻を突くほどの薬草の匂いが立ちのぼっている。
prompt.prompt_jp: 湯呑から___鼻を突くほどの薬草の匂い___立ちのぼっている。
prompt.prompt_en: The second blank marks the smell. Which particle fits?

feedback.correct_en: This is a descriptive scene introducing a new perceptual observation (the smell rising). New-information subjects of 'there is / is happening' sentences take が.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would mark the smell as an already-known topic, which clashes with this fresh, descriptive narration. も (also) has no comparative referent here.

contrast_examples.jp: 窓から光が差している
contrast_examples.en: Light is streaming in from the window (new description → が)
That light is warm (known topic → は)

prompt.context_jp: 渚: 「ホントに 放射線科医として 働く気___ないの？」
prompt.prompt_jp: 放射線科医として 働く気___ないの？
prompt.prompt_en: Nagisa asks Igarashi whether he really has no intention to work as a radiologist.

feedback.correct_en: With negative existence (〜ない), the subject is routinely marked は, especially when singling it out contrastively: 'as for the intention (to work as a radiologist), you have none?' Here Nagisa isolates and highlights that particular 気.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would sound like neutral new-information reporting, odd in this probing, slightly reproachful question. を doesn't fit ない.

contrast_examples.en: I have no time (negated topic → は)
There's no time! (sudden exclamation → が possible but different nuance)

prompt.context_jp: 五十嵐: 「技師の撮る 良質な画像___なければ 正確な診断は できないと思うんです」
prompt.prompt_jp: 技師の撮る 良質な画像___なければ 正確な診断は できない
prompt.prompt_en: Igarashi says that without good images, diagnosis is impossible.

feedback.correct_en: In the conditional 〜がなければ ('if there isn't X'), the existing/missing thing is marked with が. This is the fixed existential pattern. Note how 診断は at the end carries the contrastive topic.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would clash with the existential/conditional 'if ~ did not exist' construction. も would mean 'also not', changing the meaning.

contrast_examples.jp: 水がなければ生きられない
contrast_examples.en: We can't live without water (existential conditional → が)
As for water, there is some (topic → は)

prompt.context_jp: 渚: 「あなたの気持ち___分かったわ でも 見えすぎる あなた___見えないふりなんて できるのかしら？」
prompt.prompt_jp: あなたの気持ち___分かったわ
prompt.prompt_en: 'I understood your feelings, but...' Which particle fits the first blank?

feedback.correct_en: The は here sets 'your feelings' up as a contrastive topic — she accepts them, BUT (でも) there's a catch. The contrastive は perfectly cues the pivot that follows.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would sound like a fresh, neutral statement without the 'yes, but' shading. を is wrong because 分かる is intransitive.

contrast_examples.jp: 話は分かったが、賛成はできない
contrast_examples.en: I understand your point, but I can't agree (contrastive は)
Suddenly the meaning became clear (new realization → が)

prompt.context_jp: 小野寺: 「ただの成長痛ならいいんだけどな 俺の息子___ 昔 よく痛がってたよ」
prompt.prompt_jp: 俺の息子___ 昔 よく痛がってたよ
prompt.prompt_en: Onodera is sharing a general fact about his own son's past.

feedback.correct_en: も signals 'my son too (like this patient boy) used to complain of pain.' It explicitly groups Onodera's son with the current patient, matching the sympathetic 'me too' nuance.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would introduce the son as new info without the comparison. は would merely topicalize without the 'also like him' link that the context demands.

contrast_examples.jp: うちの子も痛がってた
contrast_examples.en: My kid too used to complain of pain (grouping → も)
My kid is healthy (plain topic → は)

prompt.context_jp: 広瀬: 「前院長のお父様___ 病気で引退されてから ずっと 働きっぱなしじゃないですか」
prompt.prompt_jp: 前院長のお父様___ 病気で引退されてから
prompt.prompt_en: 'Ever since her father retired due to illness...' Which particle fits?

feedback.correct_en: Inside the subordinate clause 〜てから ('ever since ~'), the subject takes が. Subordinate clauses typically block は, which belongs to the main clause level.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would try to make 'father' the main-clause topic, but the clause really describes Amakasu-sensei's situation; the father is just the embedded subject.

contrast_examples.jp: 父が倒れてから、母は働きづめだ
contrast_examples.en: Ever since my father collapsed, mother has been working nonstop (が in subclause, は in main)
Father is well (main topic → は)

prompt.context_jp: 金田夫人: 「私___ね 閉所恐怖症なのよ」
prompt.prompt_jp: 私___ね 閉所恐怖症なのよ
prompt.prompt_en: Mrs. Kaneda explains herself emphatically.

feedback.correct_en: She's declaring 'as for ME, I'm claustrophobic' — a self-focused topic statement explaining why she needs her dog. 私は〜なのよ is the natural self-asserting pattern.
feedback.incorrect_en: 私が would sound like answering 'who is claustrophobic?' — exhaustive identification, which doesn't fit. も would add 'me too' with no antecedent.

contrast_examples.en: As for me, I love dogs (self-topic → は)
I am the culprit (exhaustive identification → が)

prompt.context_jp: 犬をつないでおいたはずの支柱には、はずされた首輪___心細く揺れていた。
prompt.prompt_jp: はずされた首輪___心細く揺れていた
prompt.prompt_en: Only the removed collar was swaying there — the dog was gone.

feedback.correct_en: だけが marks exhaustive listing — 'only the collar, and nothing else, was there swaying.' The が emphasizes that the collar is the sole remaining element of the scene.
feedback.incorrect_en: だけは would carry contrastive nuance ('the collar at least') but weakens the stark 'only this' image. も (also) contradicts the exclusive meaning entirely.

contrast_examples.en: You are the only one I can rely on (exhaustive → だけが)
You alone I trust (contrastive singling out → だけは)

prompt.context_jp: 鏑木: 「君たちは 私の顔___泥を塗ったんです」
prompt.prompt_jp: 私の顔___泥を塗ったんです
prompt.prompt_en: 'You smeared mud ___ my face' — the set phrase for 'disgraced me.'

feedback.correct_en: 顔に泥を塗る is a fixed idiom meaning 'to disgrace / cause someone embarrassment.' The face is the surface the mud is applied TO, hence に.
feedback.incorrect_en: を already marks 泥 as the object; a second を wouldn't work. で would wrongly turn 顔 into a tool/location.

contrast_examples.en: Paint on the wall (surface → に)
My reputation was disgraced (idiom → に)

prompt.context_jp: 窓の外の空___、いつもと変わらぬ色で広がっていた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 窓の外の空___けが、いつもと変わらぬ色で広がっていた
prompt.prompt_en: Only the sky remained unchanged, implying everything else had changed.

feedback.correct_en: 空だけが = 'only the sky' — the だけが construction emphasizes that in contrast to the stormy human events, exactly one thing (the sky) was unchanged. Note the sentence contains 空だけが.
feedback.incorrect_en: The other letters don't form the set construction だけが. The passage specifically singles out the sky as the sole unchanged element.

contrast_examples.en: Only the sound echoed (exhaustive → だけが)
At least the sound was audible (contrastive concession → だけは)

prompt.context_jp: 小野寺: 「ここのお医者様___ 俺たち 技師の言うことなんか 聞く耳 持たない」
prompt.prompt_jp: ここのお医者様___ 俺たち 技師の言うことなんか 聞く耳 持たない
prompt.prompt_en: Onodera is bitterly characterizing the doctors at this hospital.

feedback.correct_en: は sets 'the doctors here' as a contrastive topic — implying 'these doctors (unlike maybe others) don't listen to us.' This matches Onodera's resigned, generalizing complaint.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would introduce them as new specific info, odd for a sweeping generalization. も (also) has no comparison antecedent.

contrast_examples.en: The doctors here are cold (characterizing topic → は)
The doctor came (new arrival → が)

prompt.context_jp: 「腹部レントゲンのオーダーだ 病院の前で女性___倒れた」
prompt.prompt_jp: 病院の前で女性___倒れた
prompt.prompt_en: Reporting an emergency: a woman has collapsed in front of the hospital.

feedback.correct_en: This is pure new-information reporting of a sudden event — 'a woman collapsed!' Such event-announcement subjects always take が.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would presuppose the woman is already a known topic, inappropriate for breaking emergency news. を doesn't fit 倒れる (intransitive).

contrast_examples.en: A child is crying (fresh observation → が)
That child (we know about) is crying (known topic → は)

prompt.context_jp: 健太郎: 「僕___わがままなんて言ったから」
prompt.prompt_jp: 僕___わがままなんて言ったから
prompt.prompt_en: Kentaro is blaming himself for his mother's collapse.

feedback.correct_en: In 僕のせいだ followed by this clause, he's identifying himself as the exhaustive cause: 'because I [and no one else] said selfish things.' Reason clauses that single out the agent of fault take が.
feedback.incorrect_en: 僕は would merely topicalize and lose the self-accusing 'it was ME who' force. も (also) would illogically share the blame with someone else.

contrast_examples.en: I'm the one who did it (self-accusation → が)
As for me, I didn't do it (contrastive → は)

prompt.context_jp: 甘春: 「千葉さん 母親___ 1人だけです」
prompt.prompt_jp: 母親___ 1人だけです
prompt.prompt_en: Amakasu urges Chiba: 'A mother is one of a kind.'

feedback.correct_en: This is a generic, defining statement — 'as for a mother, there's only one.' Characterizing/defining sentences about a general subject use は.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would read like identifying one specific mother in a group, which doesn't match the general proverbial tone. も has no second item to add.

contrast_examples.en: A life is one (generic truth → は)
A life is in danger (specific event → が)

prompt.context_jp: 同僚: 「あ～あ ついに仕事場にまで ___られましたか」
prompt.prompt_jp: ついに仕事場にまで ___られましたか
prompt.prompt_en: Mockingly: a divorce form was finally delivered even to his workplace.

feedback.correct_en: 送りつける carries the negative nuance of sending something unwanted/forcefully — perfect for the wife one-sidedly mailing divorce papers to his workplace.
feedback.incorrect_en: 届け出 is 'to submit a notification' (not passive-received). 投げ入れる is literally 'throw into' and sounds too physical/odd here.

contrast_examples.jp: 請求書を送りつけられた
contrast_examples.en: I was slapped with an invoice (unwanted → 送りつける)
Send a letter (neutral)

prompt.context_jp: 口に含んだ瞬間、彼は苦さに驚きを隠しきれず、わずかに眉を___。
prompt.prompt_jp: わずかに眉を___
prompt.prompt_en: He slightly ___ his brow at the bitterness.

feedback.correct_en: 眉をひそめる is a set collocation meaning 'to furrow/knit the brow' in displeasure or discomfort — exactly fitting the bitter-tea reaction.
feedback.incorrect_en: 眉を上げる would mean raising brows in surprise, not displeasure. 眉をかける isn't a standard phrase.

contrast_examples.en: To grimace (similar negative-reaction collocation)
To knit one's brow (displeasure)

prompt.context_jp: 渚: 「くれぐれも周りには あなたが医者であることは ___ようにね」
prompt.prompt_jp: あなたが医者であることは ___ようにね
prompt.prompt_en: Nagisa warns him to make sure his secret doesn't get out.

feedback.correct_en: バレる means 'to be found out / for a secret to slip out' — perfectly colloquial for 'don't let it leak that you're actually a doctor.'
feedback.incorrect_en: 知れない / 分からない are neutral 'can't be known' and don't carry the clandestine-secret nuance Nagisa means.

contrast_examples.en: The lie gets exposed (secret leaking → バレる)
I don't understand her feelings (neutral)

prompt.context_jp: 何を言おうと結局は損をするだけだと、長い年月の間に彼は___まで学びとっていた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 長い年月の間に彼は___まで学びとっていた
prompt.prompt_en: He had learned, after many years, down to his very ___.

feedback.correct_en: 骨の髄まで ('to the marrow of one's bones') is the fixed idiom for having something burned in deeply through experience — fitting Onodera's hard-earned resignation.
feedback.incorrect_en: 心の底 ('from the bottom of one's heart') exists but doesn't collocate with 学びとる as idiomatically. 目の奥 isn't a 'learning depth' idiom.

contrast_examples.en: Soak in to the marrow (fully absorbed → 骨の髄)
Thank from the bottom of one's heart

prompt.context_jp: 待つほどに、母の顔からは___が引いていった。
prompt.prompt_jp: 母の顔からは___が引いていった
prompt.prompt_en: As she waited, the ___ drained from her mother's face.

feedback.correct_en: 血の気が引く is the fixed idiom for the color draining from someone's face — signaling shock, fear, or physical collapse. Exactly the pre-collapse moment described.
feedback.incorrect_en: 元気が引く isn't a Japanese collocation. 熱が引く means a fever subsides (positive medical sense), wrong here.

contrast_examples.en: She went pale (shock → 血の気)
The fever went down (recovery)

prompt.context_jp: 小野寺: 「俺たち 技師が ___ことじゃねえよ」
prompt.prompt_jp: 俺たち 技師が ___ことじゃねえよ
prompt.prompt_en: 'It's not something we technicians should ___.'

feedback.correct_en: 口を挟む = 'to butt in / interject into others' affairs.' Onodera is saying technicians shouldn't meddle in doctors' decisions — the exact nuance of 挟む (to wedge in).
feedback.incorrect_en: 口を開く is just 'to open one's mouth / start speaking,' neutral. 口に出す means 'to voice/utter,' lacking the 'interfering' nuance.

contrast_examples.en: Butt into someone's conversation (meddle → 挟む)
Voice one's thoughts (utter)

prompt.context_jp: 甘春: 「何かあってからでは ___んです」
prompt.prompt_jp: 何かあってからでは ___んです
prompt.prompt_en: 'If something happens, it'll be too ___.'

feedback.correct_en: 〜てからでは遅い ('too late once ~ has happened') is a set warning phrase about preempting disaster — Amakasu's exact message urging the mother to get tested now.
feedback.incorrect_en: 痛い (painful) and 悪い (bad) don't form the fixed warning construction with 〜てからでは.

contrast_examples.jp: 病気になってからでは遅い
contrast_examples.en: It'll be too late once you fall ill (fixed warning)

contrast_examples.jp: 気づいた時には遅かった
contrast_examples.en: By the time I noticed, it was too late

prompt.context_jp: 「馬の駆けっこにね 何十万も賭けられる男なんてね 相当 ___ 深いから」
prompt.prompt_jp: 相当 ___ 深いから
prompt.prompt_en: 'A man who can bet hundreds of thousands on horse races must have deep ___.'

feedback.correct_en: 懐が深い literally 'deep pocket/bosom,' idiomatically 'big-hearted, tolerant, generous.' The joke here plays on both the money sense and the character sense.
feedback.incorrect_en: 心が深い isn't a standard idiom. 腹が深い doesn't exist; 腹黒い (black-hearted) is the related idiom.

contrast_examples.en: A tolerant, big-hearted person
To get angry (another 腹 idiom)

prompt.context_jp: 五十嵐が渚に、自分は技師として扱ってほしいと頼む場面。
prompt.prompt_en: Which version sounds more natural as Igarashi's polite, humble request to Nagisa?

choices.text: ここでは あくまで 技師ということで お願いします
ここでは 絶対に 技師だから そうしてください

feedback.correct_en: あくまで 〜ということで お願いします is a soft, humble business-polite way to insist on a stance without sounding pushy — matching Igarashi's careful tone with a senior doctor.
feedback.incorrect_en: 絶対に ~ だから そうしてください sounds blunt and demanding, more like scolding a subordinate, not fitting for addressing a radiologist senior.

contrast_examples.jp: あくまで個人の意見ということで
contrast_examples.en: Just as a personal opinion, if I may (soft hedging)

contrast_examples.jp: 絶対にそうしてください
contrast_examples.en: You absolutely must do it that way (blunt order)

prompt.context_jp: 甘春が健太郎を励ます場面。
prompt.prompt_en: Which sounds more natural when reassuring a child that his mother cares about him most?

choices.text: 健太郎君のことを 一番 大事に思ってるはずだよ
健太郎君のことを 一番 大事と考えているに違いありません

feedback.correct_en: 大事に思う + はずだよ is warm, intimate, and child-friendly — matching how an adult comforts a child.
feedback.incorrect_en: 大事と考えている + に違いありません is formal/written, more like a lawyer's statement than a gentle reassurance to a boy.

contrast_examples.en: I'm sure ~ (gentle spoken reassurance)
There is no doubt that ~ (stiff written register)

prompt.context_jp: 小野寺が若手技師たちに、諦めたような口調で語る場面。
prompt.prompt_en: Which captures Onodera's resigned, casual-boss tone better?

choices.text: おとなしく 頭 下げてりゃいいの
静かに お辞儀をしていればよろしいのです

feedback.correct_en: 頭下げてりゃいいの uses contracted spoken Japanese (〜てりゃ for 〜ていれば) and casual の ending — perfect for a bitter, world-weary senior speaking to his team.
feedback.incorrect_en: お辞儀をしていればよろしいのです is overly formal, polite announcement style — totally wrong for a locker-room gripe among coworkers.

contrast_examples.jp: 黙ってりゃいいんだよ
contrast_examples.en: You just gotta shut up (casual contracted)

contrast_examples.jp: 黙っていればよろしい
contrast_examples.en: You may remain silent (stiff polite)

prompt.context_jp: 美佐子が無理に平静を装って、検査を切り上げようとする場面。
prompt.prompt_en: Which sounds more natural for a hurried but polite request from the patient?

choices.text: この後 仕事があるので 急いでもらえますか？
この後 仕事なので 急いでくれる？

feedback.correct_en: 〜てもらえますか？ is the standard polite request form appropriate between a patient and medical staff who are strangers.
feedback.incorrect_en: 〜てくれる？ is casual, used among close people; it would sound rude to hospital staff she's never met.

contrast_examples.jp: 手伝ってもらえますか
contrast_examples.en: Could you help me? (polite request to strangers)
Can you help me? (casual, close relationship)

prompt.context_jp: 小野寺の中学生の息子が、父の職場で挨拶する場面。
prompt.prompt_en: Which greeting sounds more natural from a well-mannered middle-schooler to his father's coworkers?

choices.text: 父が いつも お世話になっています
お父さんが いつも お世話していますね

feedback.correct_en: 父がお世話になっています is the fixed humble phrase used when a family member greets another's coworkers — one refers to one's own father as 父 (plain) and uses お世話になる (receive care).
feedback.incorrect_en: お父さん refers politely to someone else's father, wrong for one's own. お世話している inverts the direction (giving care, not receiving).

contrast_examples.jp: 父がお世話になっております
contrast_examples.en: My father is in your care (humble, correct direction)

contrast_examples.jp: お父様はお元気ですか
contrast_examples.en: Is your father well? (honorific, about someone else's father)
